findings.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — [P1, confidence 100] `record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` performs an exact, non-canonical lookup while email addresses are case-insensitive (`Email.downcase` is used for user lookup), so registering `BLOCK@spamfromhome.org` bypasses an administrator's `block@spamfromhome.org` rule and creates an account the blocked-email policy promises to reject.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — [P2, confidence 100] `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` is a read-modify-write without an atomic increment or optimistic lock, so simultaneous rejected registrations for the same address overwrite each other's increment and make the stored match statistics undercount block attempts.

lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — [P2, confidence 75, advisory] `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` skips `BlockedEmail.should_block?` for an address that is both explicitly blocked and rejected by the whitelist/blacklist, so `match_count` and `last_match_at` falsely say that blocked address was never attempted; although avoiding duplicate validation work is the strongest rebuttal, the model’s documented statistics are specifically meant to identify whether a blocked address was ever blocked and the explicit block match is never evaluated.

spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:9 — [P2, confidence 75, advisory] `context "blocked email" do` covers only mocked `BlockedEmail.should_block?` outcomes and omits the existing whitelist/blacklist acceptance paths now moved into `EmailValidator`, so a regression in either site-setting policy ships while the new validator spec passes; although those branches were copied from `User`, the refactor changed their owning validation mechanism and no retained or new spec verifies that the comprehensive validator still enforces both policies.

docs/tasks/task-001.md:2 — [P2, confidence 100, advisory] `Review the change.` supplies no acceptance criteria for what “comprehensive email validation” must cover (registration response/UI behavior, existing domain policies, exact blocked-email matching, and audit statistics), so reviewers can declare the task done while a required validation surface is absent; although the diff suggests an intended implementation, implementation details cannot replace an explicit requirement that makes omissions objectively checkable.

db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:3 — [P1, confidence 100] The migration changes an already-present base migration from an empty file to `create_table :blocked_emails do |t|`, so every production database that recorded version 20130724201552 as applied skips this table creation and `BlockedEmail.where` fails with a missing-table database error after deployment.

app/models/user.rb:48 — Confidence 75, P1: `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` resolves `EmailValidator`, but its only definition is `lib/validators/email_validator.rb:1` (`class EmailValidator < ActiveModel::EachValidator`), so the validator is outside the `email_validator.rb` autoload path and User loading raises `NameError: uninitialized constant EmailValidator`.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 — [P2, confidence 100, advisory] `record.save` discards a failed statistics write and still returns the record’s blocking action, so a database validation or persistence failure silently drops `match_count`/`last_match_at` for administrators investigating rejected signup attempts; although rejecting the signup remains correct, the model expressly records these audit statistics and callers receive no signal that its promised observation was lost.

app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — [P2, confidence 100] `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` performs a case-sensitive exact lookup, so a signup using `Block@spamfromhome.org` bypasses a block record stored as `block@spamfromhome.org` and lets a blocked identity create an account.

spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb:30 — [P2, confidence 100] `blocked_email.last_match_at.should be_within_one_second_of(Time.zone.now)` reads the un-reloaded Fabricator instance after `BlockedEmail.should_block?` saves a separate query result, so the statistics example fails with `last_match_at == nil` even when the production update succeeds.

spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:19 — [P2, confidence 100] `record.errors[:email].should be_present` accepts any pre-existing or incorrectly generated email error, so the blocked-email test stays green when the validator returns the wrong localized failure reason instead of `user.email.blocked`.

spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:9 — [P2, confidence 100, advisory] `context "blocked email" do` exercises neither `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` nor `SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist`, so the refactored policy branches in `EmailValidator` can reject or accept the wrong addresses while every new validator test remains green; copying the old implementation is the strongest rebuttal, but relocating the branches changes their validation integration and no retained spec covers it.

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — [P2, confidence 75, advisory] `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` skips `BlockedEmail.should_block?` for an address that is both explicitly blocked and rejected by the whitelist/blacklist, so `match_count` and `last_match_at` falsely say that blocked address was never attempted; although avoiding duplicate validation work is the strongest rebuttal, the model’s documented statistics are specifically meant to identify whether a blocked address was ever blocked and the explicit block match is never evaluated.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in email_validator.rb line 13, the condition `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` means that if the whitelist/blacklist check already added an error, the BlockedEmail.should_block? method is never called due to short-circuit evaluation. Looking at the BlockedEmail model's should_block? method, it increments match_count and updates last_match_at when a blocked email is found. The spec comments explicitly state 'we can see whether those emails have ever been blocked by looking at last_match_at'. So if an email is both on the domain blacklist AND in the blocked_emails table, the statistics won't be updated because should_block? is never called. This is a real logic bug where the tracking statistics become inaccurate.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:9 — [P2, confidence 75, advisory] `context "blocked email" do` covers only mocked `BlockedEmail.should_block?` outcomes and omits the existing whitelist/blacklist acceptance paths now moved into `EmailValidator`, so a regression in either site-setting policy ships while the new validator spec passes; although those branches were copied from `User`, the refactor changed their owning validation mechanism and no retained or new spec verifies that the comprehensive validator still enforces both policies.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the new email_validator_spec.rb only tests the BlockedEmail.should_block? functionality with mocks, but does not test the whitelist/blacklist logic that was moved from User#email_validator to EmailValidator. Looking at the diff, the EmailValidator class (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) contains both the whitelist/blacklist checking logic AND the BlockedEmail.should_block? check, but the spec only covers the blocked email scenarios. The whitelist/blacklist logic was previously in User model and is now in the validator, but no tests verify this refactored code path works correctly. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly refactored code.

However, the diff clearly shows this is a NEW file being created (indicated by 'new file mode' in the diff header at line 'diff --git a/db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb'). adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/user.rb:48 — Confidence 75, P1: `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` resolves `EmailValidator`, but its only definition is `lib/validators/email_validator.rb:1` (`class EmailValidator < ActiveModel::EachValidator`), so the validator is outside the `email_validator.rb` autoload path and User loading raises `NameError: uninitialized constant EmailValidator`.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that EmailValidator won't be autoloaded because it's in lib/validators/email_validator.rb. However, in Rails applications, the lib directory (and subdirectories) is typically added to the autoload paths. The file follows Rails naming conventions: EmailValidator class in email_validator.rb. The validator is being used in the User model with 'validates :email, email: true', which is standard Rails custom validator syntax. Rails will look for EmailValidator when this validation runs. The finding assumes the lib/validators path isn't in autoload paths, but this is a standard Rails configuration that most applications include. Without seeing the application.rb config, we cannot verify this is actually a bug - it's a speculative concern about Rails autoloading configuration.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 — [P2, confidence 100, advisory] `record.save` discards a failed statistics write and still returns the record’s blocking action, so a database validation or persistence failure silently drops `match_count`/`last_match_at` for administrators investigating rejected signup attempts; although rejecting the signup remains correct, the model expressly records these audit statistics and callers receive no signal that its promised observation was lost.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that `record.save` in BlockedEmail.should_block? doesn't check its return value, so if the save fails (due to validation or database issues), the match_count/last_match_at statistics would be silently lost. This is a real code quality issue - the model explicitly tracks these audit statistics but doesn't handle save failures. However, this is not a bug in the strict sense because: 1) The blocking decision itself is still correct (based on action_type), 2) The primary functionality (blocking emails) works correctly, 3) Only the audit/statistics tracking would be affected. It's an important observation about silent failure handling for audit data, but not a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — [P2, confidence 100] `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` performs a case-sensitive exact lookup, so a signup using `Block@spamfromhome.org` bypasses a block record stored as `block@spamfromhome.org` and lets a blocked identity create an account.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` in the new `blocked_email.rb` model performs a case-sensitive lookup by default in most databases. The diff shows this is the exact code being added, and email addresses are case-insensitive by RFC standards. A user could bypass the block by using different casing (e.g., 'Block@spamfromhome.org' vs 'block@spamfromhome.org'). This is a real security defect in the new blocking functionality.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb:30 — [P2, confidence 100] `blocked_email.last_match_at.should be_within_one_second_of(Time.zone.now)` reads the un-reloaded Fabricator instance after `BlockedEmail.should_block?` saves a separate query result, so the statistics example fails with `last_match_at == nil` even when the production update succeeds.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the test code in spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb, the shared example 'when a BlockedEmail record matches' checks `blocked_email.reload.match_count` (with reload) but then checks `blocked_email.last_match_at` without reload. In the `should_block?` method (app/models/blocked_email.rb:11-17), a separate record is fetched via `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, modified, and saved. This is a different object instance than the Fabricator's `blocked_email`. The test correctly reloads for `match_count` but fails to reload for `last_match_at`, so `last_match_at` would still be nil from the original Fabricator instance. This is a real test bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:19 — [P2, confidence 100] `record.errors[:email].should be_present` accepts any pre-existing or incorrectly generated email error, so the blocked-email test stays green when the validator returns the wrong localized failure reason instead of `user.email.blocked`.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a test quality issue. Looking at the diff, the test in spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:19 uses `record.errors[:email].should be_present` which only checks that some error exists on the email field, not that it's specifically the 'blocked' error message. The validator in lib/validators/email_validator.rb can add different error messages: 'user.email.not_allowed' for whitelist/blacklist violations and 'user.email.blocked' for BlockedEmail matches. The test would pass even if the wrong error message was added. This is a legitimate test coverage concern - the test should verify the specific error message to ensure the blocked email path returns the correct localized message.
